definition: Widely known and admired for an achievement, skill or quality.
example: The coastal village is renowned for its hand-painted pottery.
nuance: Renowned means famous for something admirable, while notorious means famous for something bad.
prompt: For decades, a small bakery has drawn customers from all across the region.
options: The bakery is renowned for its rye bread, which people drive for hours to buy.
When the lease ran out, the owner had the bakery's contract renowned for five more years.
The bakery is so renowned that almost nobody outside its own street has heard of it.
The bakery became renowned after inspectors found mice running through its kitchen.
reasons: Wide fame earned through a quality that people admire fits the word exactly.
This confuses the word with renewed; a contract is extended, not made famous.
Being unknown beyond one street is obscurity, the reverse of wide fame.
Fame for a disgraceful reason is notoriety; the word implies admiration.

practice.prompt: Experts around the world cite a scientist's research on coral reefs.
options: Her renowned findings were unknown to everyone except her lab partner.
The biologist renowned her grant application so the funding would continue next year.
The researcher was renowned for repeatedly inventing data in her published papers.
The renowned marine biologist was invited to give the opening lecture at the conference.
reasons: Work known to just one person has no wide reputation at all.
This mistakes the adjective for the verb renew, which means to extend.
Being known for dishonesty is notoriety, not the admiring fame the word suggests.
An invitation to open a major event reflects broad respect for her work.
